items.stem: Which process changes liquid water at the surface of a puddle into water vapour?
options: Evaporation
Condensation
Freezing
Melting

explain.why: Condensation changes water vapour into liquid water, the opposite change.
Freezing changes liquid water into ice.
Melting changes a solid, such as ice, into liquid water.

solution: Evaporation is the change of liquid water into water vapour at its surface.

items.stem: Which day is the best for drying wet clothes quickly?
options: A cool day with no wind
A cool and windy day
A hot day with no moving air at all
A hot and windy day

explain.why: Cool, still air gives the slowest drying.
Wind helps, but the cool air slows evaporation.
Heat helps, but there is no wind to carry the vapour away.

solution: Heat and wind both speed up evaporation.

items.stem: Two identical wet towels are hung in the same sunny spot as shown. Which towel will dry first?
options: Q, because it is thicker and holds more heat
Q, because its water is packed close together
P, because more of its water is exposed to the air
Both dry at the same time because they are in the same place

explain.why: A thick folded towel hides most of its water from the air, so it dries slower.
Packed water has less surface in contact with the air.
The shape matters. The spread towel has a larger exposed surface.

solution: The spread-out towel P shows a larger surface to the air, so it dries faster.

items.stem: Which statement about evaporation is correct?
options: It happens only when water boils
It can happen at room temperature
It happens only when water is in sunlight
It changes water vapour into liquid water

explain.why: Water evaporates at any temperature. Boiling is faster, but evaporation does not wait for it.
Water also evaporates in the shade.
That is condensation.

solution: Water evaporates from its surface at any temperature.

items.stem: After a sunny afternoon, a puddle on a road has gone. Where did the water go?
options: It became vapour and went into the air
It sank down into the hard road
It changed into tiny pieces of ice
It was destroyed by the heat of the Sun

explain.why: A road is hard and does not soak up a puddle.
The day was hot, so the water did not freeze.
Matter is not destroyed. The water changed state.

solution: The water evaporated into water vapour.

items.stem: Which of the following would increase the rate of evaporation of water in a bowl?
options: Putting a lid on the bowl
Moving the bowl to a colder place
Pouring the water into a narrow tall cup
Blowing air across the water with a fan

explain.why: A lid traps the water vapour above the water.
A colder place slows evaporation.
A narrower surface is smaller, so evaporation is slower.

solution: Moving air carries away water vapour, so evaporation is faster.

items.stem: Two containers hold the same amount of water and are left in the same place, as shown. Which has less water left after 5 hours?
options: B, because its water is deeper and stores more heat
B, because its sides are taller
A, because more of its water touches the air
They are the same, as they hold equal water

explain.why: Depth does not speed up evaporation. Surface area does.
Tall sides do not help the water evaporate.
Equal amounts of water do not mean equal exposed surface.

solution: A is wider, so it has the larger exposed surface and loses water faster.

items.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water. A fan blows over dish A, as shown. Which dries up first?
options: B, because still air keeps the water warm
A, because moving air carries the vapour away
A, because the fan makes the water hotter
They dry up together, as the dishes are the same

explain.why: Still air lets vapour build up above the water, so B is slower.
A fan does not heat the water.
Wind is the one difference, and it speeds up evaporation.

solution: Moving air removes the water vapour at the surface, so A dries first.

items.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water. One is in a sunny spot and one in a shady spot, as shown. Which loses more water in 4 hours?
options: A, because the heat of the Sun warms its water
B, because the shade is a cooler and calmer place
B, because the Sun makes its water heavier
Both lose the same amount of water

explain.why: Cooler places slow evaporation down.
The Sun does not add mass to water.
The Sun makes one dish warmer, so it loses water faster.

solution: A is warmer, so its water evaporates faster.

items.stem: Why do we hang washing in an open, airy place instead of in a closed cupboard?
options: Moving air makes the water in the clothes boil
Clothes dry faster because the cupboard has no light
The cupboard adds more water to the clothes
Moving air carries away the vapour, so it dries faster

explain.why: Air does not make the water boil.
Light is not what dries the clothes. Moving air and warmth are.
A cupboard does not add water. It just stops the vapour leaving.

solution: Wind carries away the water vapour from the clothes.

items.stem: Where should Mei hang her wet shoes so that they dry quickly?
options: Inside a closed shoe cupboard
Inside a plastic bag in the shade
Near a sunny window where air can move
In a dark, cold storeroom

explain.why: A closed space has no moving air.
The bag traps the vapour and the shade is cooler.
Cold, still air slows evaporation.

solution: A warm, breezy place makes the water evaporate fastest.

items.stem: Salt is made from seawater in wide, shallow pans left under the Sun. Why are the pans wide and shallow?
options: The salt sinks to the bottom faster in a deep pan
A large surface lets the water evaporate quickly
A shallow pan makes the water freeze
A wide pan makes the seawater less salty

explain.why: Depth does not help the water to leave.
Pans are left in the Sun so that water evaporates, not freezes.
The amount of salt does not change. Only the water leaves.

solution: More of the water is exposed to the air and the Sun, so it evaporates faster.

items.stem: Two same pots hold 200 ml of water each. After one day, the pot with a lid has more water left. Why?
options: The lid stops the vapour escaping
The lid stops the Sun from heating the water
The lid adds water to the pot
The lid makes the water too cold to evaporate

explain.why: The pots may be in the same place and heat is not the main cause.
A lid does not add water.
Water at any temperature can evaporate.

solution: With a lid, the water vapour stays trapped, so less water is lost.

items.stem: Mei wants to find out if wind affects how fast water evaporates. Which two set-ups should she compare?
options: A and C
B and C
C and D
A and B

explain.why: A and C differ in temperature, not in wind.
B and C differ in both fan and temperature.
C and D differ in both temperature and amount of water.

solution: A and B are the same except for the fan.

items.stem: Which apparatus is best for finding how much water is left in a dish after 3 hours?
options: A thermometer put into the dish
A ruler held next to the dish
A measuring cylinder
A stopwatch started with the test

explain.why: A thermometer measures temperature.
A ruler measures length.
A stopwatch measures time.

solution: A measuring cylinder measures the volume of water.

items.stem: Each dish had 100 ml of water at first. The bar chart shows the water left after 4 hours. Which dish lost the most water?
options: R
Q
P
S

explain.why: R has the tallest bar, which means the most water is left, so it lost the least.
P kept 70 ml, so it lost 30 ml, less than Q.
S kept 55 ml, so it lost 45 ml, less than Q.

solution: Q has the shortest bar. It kept 40 ml, so it lost 60 ml.

items.stem: Cup X is left in a hot kitchen and cup Y in a cold room. Both are the same and hold the same amount of water. After one day, which has less water?
options: Cup X, because it is warmer
Cup Y, because it is colder
Both have the same amount of water
Neither, because water cannot leave a cup

explain.why: Evaporation is slower in a colder place.
The two places differ in temperature, so the loss differs.
Water vapour can leave from the open top.

solution: Higher temperature means faster evaporation.

items.stem: On a hot, dry day the water level in a pond drops. What mainly causes this?
options: Condensation of the water
Boiling of the pond water
Freezing of the pond water
Evaporation of the water

explain.why: Condensation would add water, not remove it.
A pond is far below boiling temperature.
A hot day does not freeze water.

solution: Water evaporates from the pond surface and joins the air as water vapour.

items.stem: Mrs Tan's kitchen floor is wet. Which action helps the floor dry fastest?
options: Covering the floor with a plastic sheet
Closing all the windows and doors
Switching on a fan to blow air over the floor
Switching on a freezer next to the floor

explain.why: A cover traps the vapour.
Closing up stops the air from moving.
A colder place slows evaporation.

solution: Moving air carries away the vapour, so the floor dries faster.

items.stem: From which part of a dish of water does evaporation take place?
options: The bottom of the dish
The surface of the water
Only the sides of the dish
Only the middle of the water

explain.why: Vapour leaves at the top where water meets the air.
The sides do not matter. The surface does.
All of the surface can lose water.

solution: Water changes into vapour where it meets the air, at the surface.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of evaporation?
options: Wet footprints on warm ground slowly vanish
Droplets form on the outside of a cold glass
Water turns into ice in a freezer
Steam turns into drops on a pot lid

explain.why: That is condensation.
That is freezing.
That is condensation.

solution: The water of the footprints changes into water vapour.

items.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water. Dish Q is covered with a lid, as shown. Which loses less water in one day?
options: P, because its water is cooler
P, because the lid draws water out of Q
Both lose the same amount of water
Q, because the vapour cannot escape

explain.why: The uncovered dish is not cooler in any way shown.
A lid does not draw water out.
The lid is the one difference and it slows the loss.

solution: The lid traps the vapour, so Q loses less water.

items.stem: Ali wants his wet hair to dry quickly. Which is the best way?
options: Covering it with a plastic cap
Sitting in a cold, closed room alone
A hair dryer blowing warm air
Tying it into a tight bun

explain.why: The cap traps the vapour.
Cold, still air is slow.
A bun hides most of the hair from the air.

solution: Warm, moving air makes the water evaporate faster.

items.stem: Which wet cloth will take the longest time to dry?
options: A cloth spread out on a hot, windy open balcony
A cloth folded up in a closed box in a cool room
A cloth spread out under a fan in a warm room
A cloth hung open in a warm, sunny room

explain.why: This is the fastest way to dry.
Moving air makes it dry fast.
Heat and a wide surface make it dry fast.

solution: Folded, closed in and cool: every factor slows the evaporation.

items.stem: Why should wet clothes on a line be hung with space between them?
options: More of each cloth is exposed to moving air
The clothes weigh less when they are apart
The Sun can freeze the clothes if they touch
Touching clothes stop the water from existing

explain.why: The clothes weigh the same however they hang.
Heat does not freeze clothes.
Water does not stop existing. It just leaves slower.

solution: Space lets air reach more of the wet surface.

items.stem: Ali tests how the width of the dish affects the speed of evaporation. Which two set-ups should he compare?
options: A and B
B and C
C and D
A and D

explain.why: B and C differ in temperature, not in width.
C and D differ in the fan, not in width.

items.stem: In salt farms, seawater is led into very wide, shallow ponds in sunny places. Which pair of reasons explains this best?
options: A deep pond heats up too fast and the water boils
A big surface and the Sun's heat both speed up evaporation
A shallow pond stops the wind and stores the salt
Wide ponds help the Sun freeze the salt out

explain.why: Evaporation, not boiling, removes the water.
Wind helps evaporation and the pond does not stop it.
Salt is left behind when the water evaporates.

solution: Wide ponds expose more water, and the Sun warms it.

items.stem: Wet clothes are hung in a small bathroom with the door and window shut. They dry slowly. Which is the main reason?
options: There is no moving air to carry the vapour away
There is no light to dry the clothes
The clothes weigh more in a small room
Evaporation cannot happen indoors

explain.why: Light itself does not dry clothes.
Weight does not change with the room.
Evaporation happens indoors too, only slower here.

solution: Without moving air, the vapour stays near the clothes.

items.stem: The same amount of water is poured into a wide dish and a tall, narrow cup and left side by side. After a day, the cup has more water left. Why?
options: The cup is taller and the water is deeper
The dish makes the water hotter
The cup has less water at first
The dish has a larger exposed surface

explain.why: Deeper water does not slow evaporation by being deep. The small surface does.
Both are in the same place, so the temperature is the same.
The question says the amounts are the same.

solution: Evaporation takes place at the surface, so the wider dish loses water faster.

items.stem: Two identical beakers hold the same amount of water. One is placed near a heater and one in a cool room. Which statement is correct?
options: The water in the cool room evaporates faster
Only the water near the heater evaporates
The water near the heater evaporates faster
The two evaporate at the same rate

explain.why: Heat speeds up evaporation.
Water evaporates in a cool room too, only slowly.
The places differ in temperature, so the rates differ.

solution: Higher temperature gives faster evaporation, but evaporation still happens in the cool room.

items.stem: Zara says, "Water in an open cup inside a cold refrigerator cannot evaporate." What is the best reply?
options: She is right, because evaporation only needs boiling
It does evaporate, but more slowly than in a warm room
She is right, because evaporation needs sunlight
It evaporates faster because it is cold

explain.why: Evaporation takes place at any temperature.
Sunlight is not needed.
Cold slows evaporation.

solution: Evaporation is slower in the cold but is never zero.

items.stem: Which statement tells evaporation and boiling apart correctly?
options: Evaporation is at the surface at any temperature, and boiling is throughout the liquid
Evaporation happens only below 50 °C, and boiling happens only above it
Evaporation makes liquid water, and boiling makes water vapour
Evaporation needs a fan to start it, and boiling does not

explain.why: Evaporation also takes place at higher temperatures.
Both give water vapour from liquid water.
A fan only makes evaporation faster.

solution: Evaporation is a surface change at any temperature. Boiling is rapid vapour formation in the whole liquid.

items.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water and sit in the same place. Dish Q has a lid. After 6 hours, which is correct?
options: Dish Q has less water left than dish P
Both have the same amount left
Dish Q has no water left
Dish P has less water left than dish Q

explain.why: The lid keeps the vapour in, so Q loses less.
The lid is the one difference and slows the loss.
A covered dish loses water slowly.

solution: The lid traps the vapour, so Q loses less.

items.stem: Ben pours 100 ml of water each into a tray and a tall cup and leaves them in the Sun for 5 hours. The cup has more water left. What does this show?
options: A smaller exposed surface gives slower evaporation
Tall containers make water heavier
Water evaporates only from wide containers
Trays make water boil in the Sun

explain.why: The mass of water does not depend on the container.
It evaporates from every open container.
The water is not boiling.

solution: The cup's surface is smaller, so less water leaves.

items.stem: A wet shirt is rolled into a tight ball and another is hung with the sleeves spread. Why does the rolled one dry more slowly?
options: The rolled shirt is hotter inside
Water cannot evaporate from cloth that is rolled
The spread shirt is heavier so it loses more
Most of its water is hidden from the air

explain.why: It is not hotter. Its water is just covered.
It evaporates, but only from the outside.
Weight is not the reason.

solution: The tight roll exposes a small surface, so it dries slowly.

items.stem: Mei compares a towel spread in the Sun with a towel folded in the shade to see if the area exposed matters. Why is this not a fair test?
options: Both towels are made of the same kind of cloth
She is using only two towels in the test
Both the area and the temperature are different
The towels are both wet at the very start

explain.why: Equal cloth is correct for a fair test.
Two towels are enough for a comparison.
They should both be wet at the start.

solution: Two things differ, so we cannot tell which one caused the difference.

items.stem: A fan blows over a wet cloth. Why does the cloth dry faster?
options: The fan heats the water in the cloth
The air carries away the vapour as it forms
The fan pushes the water out of the cloth
The fan turns the water into ice first

explain.why: A fan blows air. It does not heat the water.
The water leaves as vapour, not pushed as liquid.
Freezing is not part of drying.

solution: Moving air takes away vapour, so more water can evaporate.

items.stem: Which action would slow down the evaporation of a dish of water the most?
options: Covering it and placing it in a cool room
Placing it in a cool room and leaving the lid off
Covering it with a lid and leaving it in the Sun
Pouring it into a wider dish in a cool room

explain.why: This slows evaporation, but less than doing both.
This slows evaporation, but less than doing both.
A wider surface speeds up evaporation.

solution: A lid and a cool place each slow evaporation. Together they slow it the most.

items.stem: Dish A is wide and has no fan. Dish B is narrow and has a fan. Both hold the same amount of water. Why can Ali not conclude from this test that wind makes water evaporate faster?
options: The two dishes hold the same amount of water
A fan is not needed for a test
Dish A will dry faster, so the fan has no effect
Both the dish width and the fan are different

explain.why: This is correct for a fair test.
A fan is a good way to make wind.
The dishes also differ in width, so no conclusion is possible.

solution: Two variables are changed, so any difference could be due to either.

options: The shady puddle dries first because it is cooler
They dry together because they are the same size
The sunny puddle dries first because it is warmer
The sunny puddle dries by boiling away

explain.why: Cooler places slow evaporation.
The temperature differs, so the speed differs.
The puddle does not reach boiling temperature.

solution: More heat gives faster evaporation.

items.stem: The graph shows two dishes with the same water at first. One has a lid and the other does not. Which is the dish with the lid?
options: Y, because it loses the most water
X, because it loses very little water
Y, because its line falls steadily
X, because its line starts at the top

explain.why: A lid stops water from leaving, so the lid dish loses little.
A falling line means water is leaving freely.
Both lines start at the same point.

solution: X is almost flat, so the vapour was held in by the lid.

A fan can only dry solid things
The water has been frozen by the moving air
Evaporation does not happen at room temperature

explain.why: A fan helps liquids evaporate when the vapour can leave.
Moving air does not freeze water.
It does at any temperature.

solution: A closed bottle keeps the vapour in, so the level stays almost the same.

items.stem: A pot of water is at 25 °C. Another pot is boiling at 100 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Water evaporates only in the boiling pot, and not at 25 °C
Water in the 25 °C pot cannot become vapour at all
Bubbles of vapour form inside both of the pots
Both pots evaporate, and bubbles form inside only the boiling one

explain.why: Water at 25 °C also evaporates from its surface.
It slowly does.
Only the boiling water has vapour bubbles throughout.

solution: Evaporation is at the surface at any temperature. Boiling also forms bubbles inside.

Moving the pan from the shade into full sun
Building high walls around the pan to block the wind
Letting the wind blow across the pan

explain.why: A thin layer has a large surface, which speeds it up.
More heat speeds it up.
Wind speeds it up.

solution: Blocking the wind leaves vapour above the water, so evaporation is slower.

A, B and C all together

solution: A and C are blown by a fan and differ only in width.

Less than 40 ml
Exactly 40 ml
None

explain.why: A higher temperature speeds up evaporation.
The temperature is different, so the loss differs.
Water still evaporates at 40 °C.

solution: Higher temperature means more water lost in the same time.

D
B

solution: B is cooler, has no fan and has the smallest surface.

Only the width of the dish changed the rate

items.stem: Ali tests how wind affects evaporation using two dishes of water. Which of these must be kept the same in both dishes?
options: The speed of the air moving over the dish
The width of the dish
Whether a fan is blowing at the dish
The amount of water left after 3 hours

explain.why: This is the variable Ali changes.
This is the variable Ali changes.
This is what Ali measures. It is expected to differ.

solution: Everything except the wind must stay the same, including the dish width.

items.stem: Mei changes the width of the dish to see how it affects evaporation. What should she measure?
options: The water left in each dish after the same time
The width of each dish, which she changes
The temperature of the room around the dishes
The number of dishes that she is using

explain.why: She changes the width. She does not measure it as the result.
The temperature is kept the same.
This does not show how fast the water evaporated.

solution: The result is shown by how much water has been lost in the same time.

items.stem: A heap of wet clothes stays damp in a basket for days, but the same clothes hung out dry in a few hours. What is the main reason?
options: The clothes in the basket weigh less than the hung ones
The basket makes the water in the clothes more salty
Clothes cannot lose water when it is dark inside
Little water is exposed, and air does not move over it

explain.why: Weight is not the cause.
The water does not become salty.
Evaporation does not need light.

solution: A heap hides its water and has no wind, so it dries slowly.

items.stem: The same volume of rainwater is spread thinly over a large car park and also collected in a narrow bucket in the same Sun. Which dries first and why?
options: The bucket, because its water is deeper than the layer
The bucket, because its sides keep the water warm
The car park, because its thin layer has a large surface
They dry at the same time

explain.why: Deeper water does not dry faster.
The sides do not speed things up.
The surfaces differ greatly.

solution: A large surface exposes more water to the air.

items.stem: Wei pours 100 ml of water each into a narrow beaker and a wide tray in the Sun. After 2 hours, the beaker has 92 ml and the tray has 70 ml. How much more water evaporated from the tray than from the beaker?
options: 30 ml
22 ml
8 ml
162 ml

explain.why: 30 ml is the water lost from the tray only.
8 ml is the water lost from the beaker only.
162 ml adds the water that is left, which is not a loss.

solution: Tray lost 100 - 70 = 30 ml. Beaker lost 100 - 92 = 8 ml. 30 - 8 = 22 ml.

items.stem: A dish of water dries up in 10 hours at 30 °C and in 6 hours at 40 °C. Everything else is the same. Which is the best prediction for 50 °C?
options: Less than 6 hours
More than 6 hours
Exactly 6 hours
Exactly 2 hours

explain.why: Heat speeds up evaporation.
Temperature has an effect.
We cannot be sure of an exact time. The safe claim is that it is shorter.

solution: A higher temperature makes it faster, so the time is shorter.

items.stem: A beaker of water is placed on a hot plate that is switched on, before the water reaches boiling point. Compared with an identical beaker on a bench, what is true?
options: No water evaporates until the water starts to boil
The beaker on the bench evaporates faster than the other
The two beakers evaporate at the same rate as each other
The beaker on the hot plate loses water faster

explain.why: Evaporation happens before boiling.
Heat speeds up evaporation.
The hot plate warms the water, so it evaporates faster.

solution: Warm water evaporates faster, even before it boils.

items.stem: Zara puts 100 ml in dish A and 150 ml in dish B, and puts a fan by B only. She wants to test the effect of the fan. How can she improve the test?
options: Use dishes of different widths
Put the two dishes in different places
Pour equal amounts into both dishes
Measure the dishes after different times

explain.why: A different width adds a second changed variable.
A different place adds a second changed variable.
Different times make the results unfair.

solution: Only the fan should differ, so the water amount must be equal.

items.stem: Dishes A and B are the same size and are in the same place. Which statement about the graph is correct?
options: B evaporated faster because it ran out first
Both evaporated at the same rate, but B started with less water
A evaporated faster because it has more water left
A did not evaporate at all

explain.why: Both lose 15 ml each hour.
More water left does not mean faster loss.
A's line goes down, so it did evaporate.

solution: Both lines have the same steepness: 15 ml per hour.
